These leaks, whether large or small, accumulate and can allow a substantial amount of heated or cooled air escape. By reducing air leaks, air sealing improves indoor comfort, maintains more stable temperatures, and reduces the workload on the heating and cooling system. Air sealing is especially important in older homes, which typically have more leaks (Alliance, 2025). Refer to the air sealing documentation for more information on common leakage points, and best practices for sealing, and prescriptive air leakage rates based on climate zones (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025a). Attic Floor Insulation Insulating the attic floor reduces heat transfer between the living space and the unconditioned attic. In colder climates, this keeps heat inside during winter. In warmer climates, it helps keep the living space cooler. The effectiveness of insulation is measured by its R-value; a higher R- value indicates better resistance to heat flow. Installing insulation in existing homes typically involves blowing loose-fill insulation over the attic floor, especially in unfinished attics. The optimal insulation level depends on the climate zone and the home’s existing insulation. Refer to the attic insulation documentation for guidance on recommended R-values and installation approaches (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b). Duct Sealing and Insulation Ducts distribute heated or cooled air throughout the house. In many homes, especially older ones, these ducts have leaks that allow conditioned air to escape into unconditioned or semi- conditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces. As a result, the system must work harder and use more energy to maintain the desired temperature. Duct sealing addresses these leaks using mastic, metal tape, or an aerosol-based sealant, depending on the situation. Sealing ducts improves system efficiency, maintains more consistent room temperatures, and enhances indoor air quality by preventing dirty attic or crawlspace air from entering the ducts. Duct sealing can also reduce unintentional pressure imbalances, which may cause indoor air quality or combustion safety concerns. See the duct sealing documentation for more information on methods and materials (Lou & Liu, 2025). 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1.2 Technical Measure Details To maximize energy efficiency and based on building science principles, the correct order for implementing this upgrade package is: (1) advanced air sealing, (2) duct sealing, and (3) attic floor insulation. Reducing air leakage is the foundation of energy efficiency. It helps control indoor temperatures and moisture and improves the effectiveness of insulation and HVAC systems. Sealing leaks before adding insulation ensures the insulation performs as intended. It also makes leaks easier to identify and reduces the burden on field staff, since they are not working around additional insulation. Once air sealing targets are met, it is essential to address the HVAC system by sealing any leaky ducts to prevent the loss of conditioned air, particularly in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawlspaces.
